opus-5.5.text:
I think end users are going to play a much bigger role than people anticipated even a couple of years ago. When these large foundation models first came out, there was this sense that the model is the model: it gets trained once, at enormous expense, by a handful of companies, and everybody else is just a consumer of it. What we've seen instead is that the base model is really more of a starting point, and a lot of the value, and frankly a lot of the responsibility, gets pushed downstream to the people who actually deploy it for a particular purpose.

From my perspective, coming at this from the responsible AI side, that's both an opportunity and a challenge. The opportunity is obvious. A hospital system or a law firm or a bank knows its own domain, its own data, and its own notion of what a good answer looks like far better than the model developer ever could. Whether they're doing full fine-tuning, lighter-weight adaptation, or just careful prompting and retrieval, they're encoding domain knowledge the general model doesn't have.

The challenge is that a lot of the properties we care about, like fairness, privacy, robustness, and not hallucinating, don't automatically survive that process. You can take a model that was carefully aligned and evaluated by its developer, fine-tune it on a fairly modest amount of your own data, and inadvertently undo some of those guardrails, or introduce new problems specific to your use case. So I'd argue that end users who fine-tune need to think of themselves not just as customers but as part of the model development pipeline, with corresponding obligations around evaluation.

Concretely, that means defining what you care about for your application. What does fairness mean in your setting? Which groups or subpopulations matter? What kinds of errors are costly? Then you need to actually measure those things before and after you adapt the model. There's also an important role for the providers here: giving end users better tools, benchmarks, and auditing capabilities so they're not starting from scratch every time. In the end it's a shared responsibility, and I think the field is still figuring out how to divide it sensibly.

r001.rationale: The response says responsibility is pushed downstream to deployers and that end users who fine-tune become part of the model development pipeline.

r002.rationale: It discusses fine-tuning and other adaptation methods, but does not characterize that work as qualitative hyperparameter optimization.

r003.rationale: It describes the base model as a starting point and end users adding domain knowledge, but does not explain that customization enables providers to offer a very general model.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the more interesting and underappreciated shifts that's happening right now. For most of the history of machine learning, the people building the models and the people using them were essentially the same community, or at least they were very close to each other. If you wanted a model to do something for your specific problem, you had to have a data scientist or a machine learning engineer who understood training, who understood the data pipeline, who could actually get in there and tune things.

What's different about generative AI, and large language models in particular, is that the interface for shaping the model's behavior has moved much closer to the end user. I mean, prompting is a form of optimization, right? When you iterate on a prompt, when you give the model examples, when you tell it "no, not like that, more like this," you're doing something that functionally resembles fine-tuning, except you're doing it in natural language and in real time rather than through gradient descent. And then you have things like retrieval augmentation, where a user or an organization can essentially point the model at their own documents and get something that behaves as if it had been trained on them, without anyone touching the weights.

So in that sense, I think end users are becoming much more active participants in what we'd traditionally have called the model development process. And I think that's mostly a good thing. The people who understand the use case best are the ones closest to it, and they're often not the people with the deepest technical expertise.

But I'd also say there are some things I worry about. One is that the feedback loop between users and models can be very informal and very local. When a machine learning engineer fine-tunes a model, there's usually some evaluation, some held-out data, some notion of whether you've made things better or worse. When an end user is iterating on prompts, the evaluation is often just "does this feel right to me," and that can be unreliable. You can convince yourself a model is doing what you want when really you've just found the cases where it happens to work.

The other thing, and this is closer to the work I've done on fairness and privacy, is that when you push customization out to the edges, you also push a lot of the responsibility out there. If a model is fine-tuned centrally, you can audit it, you can test it for bias, you can think about what guarantees it provides. If every user is effectively building their own variant through prompting and retrieval and whatever lightweight adaptation tools they have, that's much harder to reason about collectively. So I think there's a real question about how you preserve some of the accountability and some of the rigor while still giving people this flexibility, and I don't think we've figured that out yet.

r001.rationale: The response says end users are becoming active participants in model development and that customization pushes responsibility to them.

r002.rationale: It describes prompt iteration and examples as a form of optimization that adapts model behavior in natural language for users’ needs.

r003.rationale: It explains how users can customize a model with prompts or their documents, but does not say this lets providers offer a very general model.

astra-6.text:
I think end users have an important role, because they understand what success looks like in their own application. A general-purpose model developer can’t anticipate every context in which a model will be used. The user often knows which errors are tolerable, which are costly, and what makes an output useful.

But I’d distinguish providing that expertise from having to become an expert in fine-tuning. Sometimes what you need is a better prompt, or access to the right documents, rather than a change to the model’s parameters. The tools should make it easier for users to express their objectives and provide examples, without requiring them to understand all the machinery underneath.

And evaluation is essential. If you adapt a model to your use case, you want to know whether it actually improves on examples you haven’t already shown it. You also want to know whether that improvement comes at a cost elsewhere, including privacy or reliability. So I see this as a partnership: users supply the context and judgment, and model developers supply tools that make adaptation accessible and its consequences measurable.

r001.rationale: It assigns users responsibility for supplying use-case context, objectives, examples, and judgment in adapting models, while developers provide the tools.

r002.rationale: It does not characterize user adaptation as qualitative hyperparameter optimization; it distinguishes prompts and document access from changing model parameters.

r003.rationale: It notes that developers cannot anticipate every context, but does not explain that user customization enables providers to offer a very general model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think end users have an important role because they know what success looks like in their particular application. A general-purpose model can be very capable, but that doesn’t mean it understands the preferences, constraints, or costs of mistakes in your use case.

That role doesn’t necessarily mean everyone should be updating model weights. It might mean providing examples, supplying relevant documents, or giving feedback about which responses are useful. Fine-tuning is one tool in that broader process.

The challenge is making that customization accessible while giving users ways to evaluate whether it actually helps. You can improve performance on a narrow set of examples and introduce problems elsewhere. So I’d want users involved both in defining the objective and in testing the resulting system, with some visibility into the tradeoffs they’re making.

r001.rationale: The response says users should help define objectives and test systems, but does not state that optimization responsibility shifts onto them.

r002.rationale: It discusses examples, feedback, and fine-tuning, but does not characterize this adaptation as qualitative hyperparameter optimization.

r003.rationale: It mentions general-purpose models and customization, but does not explain that user customization enables providers to offer a very general model.
